title: The Ottomans: Masters of Three Continents

cards.h: A tiny frontier band that ended up running Cairo, Baghdad and Budapest
cards.b:
Around 1300, a Turkish chief named Osman led a small band in north-west Anatolia. Six hundred years later, his family still ruled, in a state that straddled Europe, Asia and Africa.

The Ottoman story is one of the longest in history.

In 1453, 21-year-old Mehmed II conquered Constantinople, the Byzantine capital, and made it his own (Istanbul). In 1517 Selim I beat the Mamluks and took Egypt, Syria and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

Suleiman I ruled 1520-1566. He won at Mohacs (1526) and besieged Vienna (1529) but did not take it. His navy ruled much of the Mediterranean. Turks call him Kanuni, 'the Lawgiver'.

His wife Hurrem Sultan (Roxelana), a former slave, became very powerful. The architect Sinan built the Suleymaniye Mosque (1550-57).

Under the devshirme system, Christian boys from the Balkans were taken, converted and trained as officials and elite soldiers, the Janissaries. Some rose to be grand viziers.

It was brutal for families, yet it let talented outsiders rise. Over time Janissaries became powerful and political. Sultan Mahmud II destroyed them in 1826.

The Ottomans let religious communities, the millets, manage their own affairs (the system developed over time). Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 found refuge there.

Trade, coffee and coffeehouses boomed. Yet early sultans practised fratricide: Mehmed II declared it acceptable for a new sultan to kill his brothers. Later princes were confined instead.

From the 1700s, Europe's armies and economies pulled ahead. In the 1800s the empire became 'the sick man of Europe' as it lost lands. It joined World War I on Germany's side and lost. In 1922 the sultanate was abolished, and in 1924 the caliphate.

The old view said the empire decayed after Suleiman. Newer historians say it adapted, reformed and survived 350 more years. The Tanzimat reforms (1839-76) tried to modernise.

Also, the Armenian genocide (1915-16) remains a heated issue. Many scholars and countries call it genocide; Turkey rejects that label.

Five things to remember

  1. Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.
  2. Suleiman (1520-66) was the peak.
  3. Devshirme and Janissaries shaped the state.
  4. Millets gave religious autonomy.
  5. Sultanate ended in 1922.

Think about it

  • Why do big states mix tolerance and force?
  • What caused the end: weakness, or the First World War?
